label: When God Feels Far Away
framing: There are seasons when prayer feels like talking to the ceiling and the old joy has gone cold. Scripture treats this not as proof of God's absence but as a known country of the faithful, where God is often nearest when he feels furthest, doing work below the level of feeling.
cultural: The Psalmist cried out, How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, and was not corrected for it. Israel knew literal wilderness, forty years of barren ground where God fed them daily but the manna grew tiresome. The biblical writers gave us a vocabulary for the dry season precisely because they lived through it and refused to fake their way past it.
historical: The church has named this experience for centuries. John of the Cross, in the sixteenth century, called it the dark night of the soul and insisted it was God's purifying work rather than his withdrawal. Mother Teresa lived decades in such dryness while serving faithfully, proof that the dry heart and the obedient life can run side by side.
application: Keep to the practices, prayer, Scripture, worship, when the feeling is gone, because faith is not built on the feeling and often returns through the habit. Tell God honestly that he feels distant rather than performing a closeness you do not feel. Let others pray when you cannot. And if the dryness is a heaviness that will not lift, talk with a pastor or counselor, since dryness and depression can wear the same face.

verses.text: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence? My tears have been my food both day and night, while men ask me all day long, “Where is your God?”
verses.where: Far from the temple, a worshiper thirsts for God like a deer panting for water, with tears for food and people asking him all day where his God is. The site's plain note says the singer loves God and is still low, does not pretend, and talks honestly to God and to himself. It adds that the psalm does not say why he is low, and gives no single cure.

verses.text: If I go east, He is not there, and if I go west, I cannot find Him. When He is at work in the north, I cannot behold Him; when He turns to the south, I cannot see Him. Yet He knows the way I have taken; when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold.
verses.where: Job looks east and west, north and south, and cannot find God anywhere. In the same breath he says that God knows the way he has taken, and that when he has been tested he will come out as gold. The site's note on the chapter says Job trusts that God knows his way even while he cannot see him.

verses.text: Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of His Servant? Who among you walks in darkness and has no light? Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God.
verses.where: The prophet speaks to people who fear the LORD and obey him, and still walk in darkness with no light. He does not tell them their darkness proves they are faithless. He tells them to trust in the name of the LORD and lean on their God, and warns against lighting fires of their own.

verses.text: Remember that these forty years the LORD your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments. He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat, which neither you nor your fathers had known, so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
verses.where: Moses tells Israel to remember the forty years in which God led them through the wilderness, humbled them, and fed them with manna, so that they would learn that man does not live on bread alone. The site's notes say the test was not a trap but meant to do them good in the end, and that it showed Israel to itself. Its plain note asks what you really live on.

verses.text: Then the LORD said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD. Behold, the LORD is about to pass by.” And a great and mighty wind tore into the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire came a still, small voice.
verses.where: At Horeb the LORD passes by Elijah, and he is not in the great wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still, small voice. God's presence does not always come in the form a person expects or feels most strongly. Afterward, the site's note says, God gives Elijah new work and tells him he is not alone.

verses.text: Blessed are those whose strength is in You, whose hearts are set on pilgrimage. As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs; even the autumn rain covers it with pools. They go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion.
verses.where: Pilgrims on the way to God's house pass through the Valley of Baca, a dry valley, and make it a place of springs. The site's plain note says the road to God may run through a valley of tears, and that the psalm does not say the valley is skipped; those whose strength is in God find springs there. They go from strength to strength.

verses.text: Jesus also said, “The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground. Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how. All by itself the earth produces a crop—first the stalk, then the head, then grain that ripens within.
verses.where: Jesus compares the kingdom to a man who scatters seed and then sleeps and wakes while it grows, though he does not know how. The site's note says the point falls not on the man's effort but on the growth that happens without him, and its plain note says much of God's work happens while we are not watching.

verses.text: Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus—and He disappeared from their sight. They asked each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?”
verses.where: Two disciples walk the road to Emmaus beside the risen Jesus without knowing him. Only when he breaks bread are their eyes opened, and they realize their hearts had been burning as he spoke. The site's plain note says their hearts were burning long before they understood why.

verses.text: Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
verses.where: Jesus tells his disciples to remain in him as a branch remains in the vine, because apart from him they can do nothing. The site's note says union with Christ is not a technique but a dependence, and that the command to remain is a command to keep receiving. Its plain note says the branch does not strain to produce grapes; it stays joined to the vine.

verses.text: Now this is what the LORD says— He who created you, O Jacob, and He who formed you, O Israel: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine! When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze.
verses.where: God tells Israel not to fear, because he created them, redeemed them and called them by name. He does not promise they will never pass through water or fire; he promises to be with them when they do.

misread.taken: “Your sins have hidden His face from you” is used to tell anyone who feels far from God that the distance must be their fault, so that every dry season is read as hidden sin.
misread.says: The site's note says the prophet is speaking to a society where violence, lies and injustice are everywhere, and the chapter ends with the LORD himself coming to redeem those who turn and promising that his Spirit and his words will never leave them. Sin can come between a person and God, and an honest heart will ask whether something needs confessing. But Scripture also keeps the prayers of the faithful in the dark, and the site's plain note on Psalm 42 says the singer loves God and is still low and does not say why. Feeling far is not, by itself, proof of anything.
misread.text: Surely the arm of the LORD is not too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear. But your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you, so that He does not hear.

whole: If the dryness has come with a heaviness that will not lift, with lost sleep or appetite, or with thoughts of hurting yourself, talk to a doctor and someone you trust; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, because dryness and depression can wear the same face. For many believers the dry season comes without any crisis. Prayer feels like talking to the ceiling, the Bible reads like a page of words, and songs that once moved you pass by while you go through the motions and wonder whether anyone is listening. Some carry an extra weight: the fear that the dryness means they have done something wrong, or that the faith they had was never real.

Scripture treats this as a known country of the faithful. The psalmist who thirsts for God like a deer for water has tears for food and neighbors asking where his God is. Job goes east and west and cannot find God, and says in the same breath that God knows the way he takes. Isaiah speaks to people who fear the LORD and still walk in darkness with no light. Israel spent forty years in a wilderness where God fed them every day and taught them to live on his word rather than on what they could see. The site's note on Psalm 42 says the singer loves God and is still low, and does not say why. Feeling far from God is not the same as God being far.

So the wisdom of the dry season is mostly faithfulness in small things. Keep praying, reading and gathering with God's people when the feeling is gone, because faith is not built on the feeling and often returns through the habit. Tell God honestly that he feels distant, rather than performing a closeness you do not feel; the psalms give you the words. Let others pray when you cannot. Remain, as Jesus says, rather than strain: the branch bears fruit by staying joined to the vine, not by effort. Ask honestly whether something needs confessing, without assuming it must. And if the dryness is a heaviness that will not lift, talk with a pastor and see a doctor.

God is often nearest when he feels furthest. The two disciples on the road to Emmaus walked beside the risen Jesus without knowing him, and only afterward said their hearts had been burning. Elijah met God not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire but in a still, small voice. The pilgrims of Psalm 84 do not skip the dry valley; they find springs in it and go from strength to strength. The God who led Israel through the wilderness has not stopped leading because you cannot feel his hand.
deep.sit: If you stopped measuring God's nearness by what you feel, what small practice would you keep doing this week anyway, and who could you tell where you really are?

prayer.lead: David prays from a dry and weary land. The site's plain note says that if you feel dry toward God, the longing is itself a kind of prayer, and suggests praying verses 1 to 5 first thing in the morning, as Christians have done for many centuries.
prayer.text: O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water. So I have seen You in the sanctuary and beheld Your power and glory. Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You. So I will bless You as long as I live; in Your name I will lift my hands. My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods; with joyful lips my mouth will praise You.

careLines.text: If ‘my tears have been my food both day and night’ is true of you now, please do not carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
